channel.title: The Discovery Wire
channel.description: Science, decoded — the experiments, the instruments, and the questions nobody has answered yet.

item.title: Mars Dust Is Kinder to Spacesuits Than Moon Dust — and Sneakier
item.description: Perseverance has spent 1,645 Martian days wearing tiny swatches of spacesuit fabric. The good news: Mars dust is smooth and barely wears the material. The catch: some of it is 100 nanometers wide and laced with toxic perchlorates.

item.title: In 17 Days, Light Itself Will Need a Full Day to Reach Our Farthest Machine
item.description: On November 18, 2026, NASA's Voyager 1 — launched in 1977 — will cross the one-light-day mark, 16.1 billion miles from the Sun. A signal sent that morning will not arrive until the next day.

item.title: A World Maybe 1,000 Kilometers Wide Was Hiding Beyond Pluto
item.description: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has found its first dwarf planet candidate, 2026 ED138 — a large, bright, red world beyond Neptune that sat unnoticed in survey data and in archives going back to 2016.

item.title: Something Is Watching From 7,500 Light-Years Away — Webb and Hubble Catch the Cat's Head Nebula Staring Back
item.description: Released just before Halloween, NASA's new Webb and Hubble views of the Cat's Head Nebula show a dusty pillar inside the Carina Nebula being carved by massive stars — with a newborn star for an eye.

item.title: Earthquake Watch — Five M5+ Quakes in Under Three Hours off Vanuatu
item.description: A magnitude 6.0 struck northwest of Port-Olry, Vanuatu on October 28 — the middle of a tight cluster of five magnitude 5.0-or-greater events in about two hours and 52 minutes, all shallow, all offshore, Green alert.

item.title: The asteroid crime scene is about to get its first inspector
item.description: Four years after NASA deliberately smashed a spacecraft into the asteroid Dimorphos, ESA's Hera mission has hit the brakes 2,300 kilometres out and is due to arrive on 4 November to examine the aftermath.

item.title: Astronomy magazine's 2026 astrophotography contest has its winners
item.description: More than 1,400 entries, 13 years since the last contest — and the grand prize went to "The Dementors of Cepheus," nearly 30 hours of exposure on a supernova remnant.

item.title: How a story gets onto this page — our verification pipeline
item.description: Every Discovery Wire post passes through a verification pipeline before it publishes. Here's how it works — the gates, the kill steps, and the image rules.

item.title: A Decade-Old Prediction Just Passed a 100,000-Quasar Test — Black Holes Can Be Kicked Out of Their Galaxies
item.description: Researchers at Hungary's Eötvös Loránd University found statistical evidence that merging supermassive black holes get kicked from their galactic centers — exactly the signature predicted ten years ago.

item.title: The World's Most Mysterious Manuscript May Have Been Read in the Wrong Order All Along
item.description: A new study in Digital Medievalist presents strong evidence that the Voynich Manuscript's pages were misbound — and that every attempt to decode it was working from a scrambled book.

item.title: Weekly Earthquake Watch — M7.0 Strikes Tibet
item.description: The week's largest earthquake — a magnitude 7.0 in a remote stretch of Tibet — killed at least 16 people. A 6.9 in Kamchatka and a Vanuatu swarm round out a busy seven days.

item.title: Three New Ghosts Found Haunting Cassiopeia
item.description: It took 100 hours of staring and a special oxygen filter to reveal three faint blue phantoms near the famous Ghosts of Cassiopeia — and nobody yet knows what they are.

item.title: The Mystery-Lover's Bookshelf: Three Carl Sagan Classics
item.description: Chasing cosmic mysteries? These three Sagan classics are where we'd start — the story of the universe, the toolkit for thinking clearly about it, and the reflection on our tiny place in it.

item.title: The 3,700-Year-Old Printing Press Nobody Can Read
item.description: A fired-clay disc found in a Minoan palace in 1908 carries 241 stamped symbols from 45 carved seals, spiraling across both faces — the earliest known printing, and nobody can read a word of it.

item.title: Japan Just Launched a Mission to Bring Home Pieces of a Martian Moon
item.description: JAXA's MMX spacecraft lifted off this morning for Phobos. If it works, a spoonful of a Martian moon arrives on Earth in 2031 — the first material ever returned from the Mars system.

item.title: The Galaxy Mapper That Found a Comet It Wasn't Looking For
item.description: Euclid was built to stare at two billion distant galaxies. Its first comet found it anyway — spotted by a Ph.D. student's software in images where it was never supposed to appear.

item.title: A Signal From Empty Space — Webb's Unexplained Detection in the Ultra Deep Field
item.description: In the most-mapped patch of sky in human history, Webb's spectrograph found a bright infrared signal coming from a spot where nothing is visible — and four explanations can't pin it down.

item.title: The 845-Year-Old Supernova That Just Revealed Pearls of Gas
item.description: In 1181, astronomers in Japan, China, and the Arab world recorded a "guest star" in Cassiopeia. Now Gemini North has shown its remnant strung with pearl-like knots of gas — and the "zombie star" that survived the blast.

item.title: There's a Treble Clef Hanging Over Two Colliding Galaxy Clusters
item.description: NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory just cracked the case of the "Treble Clef" — a radio formation shaped like a musical symbol, hiding almost directly behind the Milky Way.

item.title: One side of this planet is 650°C hotter than the other — and Webb just mapped it in 3D
item.description: Using a new technique called 'transmission strings,' astronomers traced the uneven shape of the hot Jupiter WASP-17b's atmosphere — finding a cooler morning limb and a blistering evening limb, 1,300 light-years away.
